title: Monsters, NPCs and AI
thesis: Across the talks the goal of roguelike AI is not a perfect opponent but a believable, readable character: players project far more intelligence than the code contains, so a few legible rules, varied per creature, beat optimal play. The same holds for NPCs: cheap state machines and toggled copies can fake purpose, while deeper simulations of needs, beliefs, relationships and plans pay off only when their output stays legible and gives the player something to act on.

sections.heading: Monsters with character: behaviour players can read and exploit
sections.brief: Open with the convergence that monsters should feel like characters, not optimal killers: Lachlan Kingsford's varied MCTS goblins, Rogue's minimal AI onto which playtesters projected behaviours that did not exist (and exploited the zigzagging bat), and Jeff Olson's regret that Alphaman's monsters all felt the same. Then show what makes behaviour legible and exploitable: Advanced Rogue's fleeing-but-cornered monsters, Glenn Wichman heading pursuers for the door, simple trigger-based enemies in Liotta's puzzle levels and Trogue, Word Processor's enemies defined by how a mouse moves, and Nauticrawl's noise-triggered enemies. Treat perception as a design lever: immersive-sim awareness models (Rich Wilson), smell as a separate sense (Benet Devereux), and Clean Sweep's multiplayer targeting rules. Then Reed Lockwood's argument that monster-trap interaction is the richest trap dimension, and stage the monster-item-use disagreement: Dungeon Crawl removed pickup because players spent fights hiding weapons, while Advanced Rogue's item-using monsters made picking up missiles a tactic, and Bloomquist wonders whether item-using persistent monsters blur into players. Close with emergent surprises (Chogue's cowardly king, Skyrim's treasure foxes, ADOM hesitation fixing four-way dodging) as a warning and an opportunity, and the open wish for learning monsters; end with guidance: give each creature a few distinct, observable rules and let the player learn them.

sections.heading: Choosing a decision architecture: state machines, trees, search and shared actions
sections.brief: A practical comparison of how to implement monster decisions, specific enough to build from. Start with finite state machines (Bloomquist tweaking transitions for personality on the C64) and Slay the Spire's Jaw Worm as a probabilistic state machine, then Johnathan Pagnutti's point that no-repeat rules duplicate states and make the graph explode. Contrast Kate Compton's decision trees as data you can log, mutate and learn, and Kingsford's MCTS: it adapts to new rules for free but gives monsters shared perfect information (frame it in fiction as an omniscient controller) and is CPU-heavy, pushing toward fewer, deeper actors. Cover the plumbing that makes AI cheaper: Bob Nystrom's Action objects shared by player and monsters, The Sims' advertise-versus-provide objects and Compton's blackboards. End on movement costs as a design constraint: Albert Ford's FOV plus jump point search, and the cautionary cases where pathfinding shaped the game (Noita's moving pixels killed its god-game concept, Brian Walker's platformer leaning on flyers, Bioloom decoupling physics legs from visuals). Guidance: pick the simplest structure that expresses the behaviours you want, keep behaviour in data, and let movement cost shape the bestiary.

sections.heading: Minds from simple parts: needs, beliefs and plans
sections.brief: Argue that believable NPC minds come from composing simple parts rather than one clever brain. Lead with Dustin Freeman's Spirit of the Ages: concerns produce intentions chosen by weighted random selection, Maslow-like priorities as probabilities, unchosen concerns escalating into obsessions, Internal Family Systems as the template, and his open questions about how learned fears should spread. Set beside it Stephen Ware's planning work: characters must act on beliefs, not full observability, model hope, fear and relief, and pick only Pareto-optimal plans or they do absurd things. Show subjectivity converging from three directions: Bad News implanting beliefs and rumours that can be misremembered, Felt characters sifting events into motivation tokens, and the Cozy Mystery Construction Kit judging crimes by personal values. Use Jeff Lait's Fatherhood (children seeking attention, so scolding backfires) as a case where a tiny mind model creates a lesson, and close with Cat Manning's warning from Prom Week that minds which shift too fast become illegible. Guidance: give each agent a few simple drives and private knowledge, and damp change so players can follow it.

sections.heading: NPCs with agendas: from toggled copies to villainous schemes
sections.brief: How to make NPCs seem to pursue goals in the world, staged as a spectrum from cheap illusion to deep simulation. Start with Nathan Savant's observation that Elden Ring fakes purposeful movement by toggling copies of an NPC, and Hades' hub respawns, then the Hobbit (Veronika Megler, via Aaron Reed) where every character plays the game by its own script. Build Savant's modular recipe: motivation decides which systems an NPC reacts to, a minimal villain is a location, animations and a trigger, plans with fixed ends and random middles, any game value as a trigger, recurring guardians, and know the story your triggers tell. Then contrast Tarn Adams' Dwarf Fortress villains: type and history goals, layered relationships, MICE-based recruitment, goals fed down a network, agreements stored as objects for exposition and blackmail, agents knowing only their link; add Jasmine Otto's multiscale faction idea. Close with 80 Days' NPCs who push back on the player (Kreminski on Meg Jayanth) and Ultima Ratio Regum's culturally driven crowd movement as texture. Guidance: begin with states and triggers tied to systems the game already has, and deepen only where the player can see the result.

sections.heading: Relationships, rivals and companions
sections.brief: Argue that per-NPC relationship state is fuel for procedural stories, and that a single linear reputation bar wastes it. The core is Jim Shepard's model: like and respect as two independent axes, their quadrants for allies and foes, personality flags that read events differently (the Paladin and Rogue splitting treasure), foes forming opinions in combat, and charm temporarily swinging values. Show convergence with Jagged Alliance's web of mercenary likes and hatreds (Brenda Romero) and Blue Lacuna's two-axis classification into twelve archetypes (Aaron Reed), and the faction view from Caves of Qud, where history-driven faction preferences and reputation turn hostile goat folk friendly. Then companions: Shepard's opt-in romance with combat-ally payoffs and consequences for unrequited affection, Qud's one-follower proselytize limit, Sersa Victory's golem bought with a ring, and Tyriq Plummer's point that human partners can engage systems no AI ally can. Guidance: track at least two dimensions, make them readable, and attach concrete gameplay consequences, opt-in where stakes are personal.

sections.heading: Talking to NPCs: conversation, expression and the limits of believability
sections.brief: The frontier: how players communicate with NPCs and when to avoid talking NPCs altogether. Open with Mark R Johnson's goal for Ultima Ratio Regum, conversations with greetings, farewells and questions back rather than kiosks, and the problem it created (optimisers interrogating every NPC) with his fix of boredom and suspicion spreading through a culture. Then Nic Junius's case that dialogue couples lines to fixed reads and gestures, and that decoupling them, treating every action as expressive, annotating gestures with affect like fighting-game frame data, and giving human and AI characters a shared physical language, opens a new axis of play. Set against this the believability limits: Tim Keenan chose logs over NPCs in Duskers because talking AI would break isolation, while G blekkenhorst found a static, self-absorbed script convinced players it was listening; add Dennis Greger's reality-TV nudges as techniques for prompting action. Guidance: either give conversation real consequences and costs, or sidestep the limits through framing.
